body.en: Chapter 3's single second-order equation \( y''+by'+cy=0 \) is secretly a special case of a more general object: a system of coupled first-order equations, tracking several interacting quantities at once (two competing populations, current and charge in a circuit, position and velocity). Linear Algebra Chapter 6's eigenvalues and eigenvectors turn out to be exactly the right tool for solving such systems in closed form — and for predicting, from the eigenvalues alone, the qualitative shape of every solution without solving anything.

A (homogeneous, constant-coefficient) linear system of two first-order equations has the matrix form \[ \mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),\qquad\mathbf{x}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}x_1(t)\\x_2(t)\end{pmatrix},\quad A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}. \] Chapter 3's single equation \( y''+by'+cy=0 \) is the special case \( x_1=y \), \( x_2=y' \): then \( x_1'=x_2 \) and \( x_2'=y''=-cy-by'=-cx_1-bx_2 \), i.e. \( A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-c&-b\end{pmatrix} \) — every technique in this chapter applies to Chapter 3's equations too, viewed this way.

label.en: ▲ Theorem 7.1 — Solution via eigenvalues (distinct real case)

body.en: If \( A \) has real, distinct eigenvalues \( \lambda_1\neq\lambda_2 \) with eigenvectors \( \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2 \) (Linear Algebra, Definition 6.1), then \[ \mathbf{x}(t)=C_1e^{\lambda_1t}\mathbf{v}_1+C_2e^{\lambda_2t}\mathbf{v}_2 \] solves \( \mathbf{x}'=A\mathbf{x} \) for any constants \( C_1,C_2 \) — and (citing the standard existence–uniqueness theorem for linear systems, which guarantees exactly one solution through each initial condition \( \mathbf{x}(0) \)) every solution has this form, since Theorem 6.1's independence of \( \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2 \) lets \( C_1,C_2 \) be chosen to match any prescribed \( \mathbf{x}(0) \).

label.en: Proof that the formula solves the system

body.en: By linearity of differentiation, it suffices to check each term \( e^{\lambda_it}\mathbf{v}_i \) individually solves \( \mathbf{x}'=A\mathbf{x} \) (then any combination does too — the same superposition idea as Chapter 3, Theorem 3.1). Differentiating (the vector \( \mathbf{v}_i \) is constant): \[ \frac{d}{dt}\big(e^{\lambda_it}\mathbf{v}_i\big)=\lambda_ie^{\lambda_it}\mathbf{v}_i. \] And \[ A\big(e^{\lambda_it}\mathbf{v}_i\big)=e^{\lambda_it}(A\mathbf{v}_i)=e^{\lambda_it}(\lambda_i\mathbf{v}_i)=\lambda_ie^{\lambda_it}\mathbf{v}_i, \] using \( A\mathbf{v}_i=\lambda_i\mathbf{v}_i \) (the defining property of an eigenvector). The two sides match, so \( e^{\lambda_it}\mathbf{v}_i \) solves \( \mathbf{x}'=A\mathbf{x} \).

label.en: Worked example 7.A — Distinct real eigenvalues (a saddle)

body.en:
Solve \( \mathbf{x}'=A\mathbf{x} \) for \( A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\4&-2\end{pmatrix} \).

Characteristic equation: \( \det(A-\lambda I)=(1-\lambda)(-2-\lambda)-4=\lambda^2+\lambda-6=(\lambda-2)(\lambda+3)=0 \Rightarrow\lambda_1=2,\;\lambda_2=-3 \) — real, opposite signs.

\( \lambda_1=2 \): \( (A-2I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf0\Rightarrow\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\4&-4\end{pmatrix}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf0\Rightarrow\mathbf{v}_1=(1,1) \).

\( \lambda_2=-3 \): \( (A+3I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf0\Rightarrow\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\4&1\end{pmatrix}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf0\Rightarrow\mathbf{v}_2=(1,-4) \).

\[ \mathbf{x}(t)=C_1e^{2t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}+C_2e^{-3t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-4\end{pmatrix}. \] As \( t\to\infty \), the growing \( e^{2t} \) term dominates and trajectories run off toward \( \mathbf{v}_1 \)'s direction; as \( t\to-\infty \), the (now-growing) \( e^{-3t} \) term dominates instead — the origin repels along one eigenvector direction and attracts along the other. This mixed behavior is exactly what "saddle point" describes.

EigenvaluesClassificationBehavior as \(t\to\infty\)
Real, same sign (both \(>0\) or both \(<0\))NodeAll trajectories move away from (source) or toward (sink) the origin
Real, opposite signsSaddleAttracted along one eigenvector, repelled along the other
Complex, nonzero real part \(\alpha\)SpiralSpirals outward (\(\alpha>0\)) or inward (\(\alpha<0\))
Purely imaginary (\(\alpha=0\))CenterClosed elliptical orbits, neither growing nor decaying

This is exactly Linear Algebra Chapter 6's diagonalization at work: the eigenvalues' real parts control growth/decay (via \(e^{\alpha t}\)) and their imaginary parts control rotation (via \(\cos\beta t,\sin\beta t\)) — precisely as in Chapter 3, Theorem 3.2's three cases, one dimension up.

Solve \( \mathbf{x}'=A\mathbf{x} \) for \( A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix} \), and classify the origin.

\( \det(A-\lambda I)=(-1-\lambda)^2+1=\lambda^2+2\lambda+2=0\Rightarrow\lambda=\dfrac{-2\pm\sqrt{4-8}}{2}=-1\pm i \) — complex, \( \alpha=-1<0 \): a stable spiral.

Eigenvector for \( \lambda=-1+i \): \( (A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf0\Rightarrow\begin{pmatrix}-i&1\\-1&-i\end{pmatrix}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf0\Rightarrow -iv_1+v_2=0\Rightarrow\mathbf{v}=(1,i) \).

Following the same real/imaginary-part extraction as Chapter 3's complex case: \( e^{(-1+i)t}(1,i)=e^{-t}(\cos t+i\sin t)\big(1,i\big) \) has real part \( e^{-t}(\cos t,-\sin t) \) and imaginary part \( e^{-t}(\sin t,\cos t) \), giving the general real solution \[ \mathbf{x}(t)=e^{-t}\Big(C_1\cos t+C_2\sin t,\;-C_1\sin t+C_2\cos t\Big). \] The \( e^{-t} \) factor shrinks every trajectory toward the origin while \( \cos t,\sin t \) rotate it — a spiral, exactly as the classification table predicts for \( \alpha=-1<0 \).

value.en: Node, saddle, spiral, or center — read straight off the eigenvalues

body.en:
Solve \( \mathbf{x}'=A\mathbf{x} \) for \( A=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix} \), and classify the origin.

Show solution

\( A \) is already diagonal, so its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries: \( \lambda_1=3 \) (eigenvector \( (1,0) \)), \( \lambda_2=-1 \) (eigenvector \( (0,1) \)).

\[ \mathbf{x}(t)=C_1e^{3t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}+C_2e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}C_1e^{3t}\\C_2e^{-t}\end{pmatrix}. \]

Real eigenvalues of opposite sign: a saddle point.

Classify the origin for \( A=\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&-5\end{pmatrix} \).

Solution: Eigenvalues \( -2,-5 \) — real, both negative.

Stable node (a sink): every trajectory approaches the origin as \( t\to\infty \).

Classify the origin for \( A=\begin{pmatrix}0&2\\-2&0\end{pmatrix} \).

Solution: \( \det(A-\lambda I)=\lambda^2+4=0\Rightarrow\lambda=\pm2i \) — purely imaginary.

Center: closed elliptical orbits around the origin, neither growing nor decaying.

question.en: Practice: Without solving, classify the origin for \( \mathbf{x}'=A\mathbf{x} \), \( A=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix} \).

solution.en: \( \det(A-\lambda I)=(1-\lambda)^2+1=0\Rightarrow\lambda=1\pm i \) — complex with real part \( \alpha=1>0 \). An unstable spiral: trajectories spiral outward, away from the origin.
